prompt: rf = 4%, E(R_M) = 10%. Stock X has a beta of 1.2 and an expected return of 13%; stock Y has a beta of 0.5 and an expected return of 6%. Compute the required return and the alpha of each stock. Which would you buy, which sell? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Required (CAPM) return: X = 4% + 1.2 × 6% = 11.2%, Y = 4% + 0.5 × 6% = 7%.
α = E(R) − required: X = 13% − 11.2% = +1.8% → buy (above the SML); Y = 6% − 7% = −1% → sell / underweight (below the SML).
Judge each stock against its own required return, never against the other stock.

steps.title: Required return of each stock (CAPM)
steps.why: The required return is what the stock must offer for its market risk (beta).

steps.title: Decision
steps.why: Positive alpha: the stock pays more than its risk requires (above the SML) → buy. Negative alpha: it pays less (below the SML) → sell or underweight.

pitfalls: Comparing X's 13% with Y's 6% – each stock is judged against its own required return.

prompt: Fenway Corp. has a beta of 1.5. An analyst expects a return of 15% over the next year. The market risk premium is 8% and the risk-free rate 4%. What is the stock's alpha? Does the analyst consider the stock over- or undervalued? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Required return = 4% + 1.5 × 8% = 16%.
α = 15% − 16% = −1% < 0 → the stock pays less than its risk requires: it is overvalued (its price is too high).

steps.title: Required return (CAPM)
steps.why: Here the market risk premium (8%) is given directly.

steps.title: Over- or undervalued?
steps.why: Negative alpha: the stock offers less than its risk requires. Investors would sell, so the price is too high today.

pitfalls: Thinking a negative alpha means "cheap" – it means the price is too high.

prompt: (a) What are Zeta's expected return, required return and alpha? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Expected return
steps.why: Return = (expected price in one year + dividend) / price today − 1.

pitfalls: Forgetting the dividend in the expected return.

basis.ref: Competition pushes alphas to zero · Folien 17–18

prompt: (b) Competition among investors pushes the alpha to zero. At what price today is Zeta's alpha exactly zero? Report the price with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
With the same expected payoff (56.50 + 2.50 = 59.00), the price must give exactly the required return:
P₀ = 59.00/(1 + 8.85%) = 54.20.
Buying pressure lifts the price from 52.00 to 54.20, which lowers the expected return to the required 8.85%.

steps.title: Idea
steps.why: Investors buy Zeta until the alpha is gone. The expected payoff in one year stays the same (59.00); only today's price rises. Alpha = 0 means the expected return equals exactly the required return of 8.85%.

steps.title: Discount the payoff at the required return
Check
steps.why: The price rises from 52.00 to 54.20, which pushes the expected return down to the required 8.85%.

pitfalls: Discounting only the price (56.50) and forgetting the dividend.

basis.ref: Trading on news: takeover offers · Folien 31–32

prompt: Target SA trades at EUR 25.00. A bidder announces an offer of EUR 34.00 per share, and Target's price jumps to EUR 31.30 the same day. If the deal fails, the price falls back to EUR 25.00. What probability of success does the market price imply? Why is the 2.70 gap not a free lunch?
modelAnswer:
31.30 = p × 34.00 + (1 − p) × 25.00 → p = 6.30/9.00 = 70.00%.
Public news is priced at once. The remaining gap of 2.70 compensates for the risk that the deal fails; buying at 31.30 is not a riskless gain.

steps.title: Set up the price as an expected value
steps.why: After the announcement, the price is the probability-weighted value of the two outcomes: success (34.00) or failure (25.00).

steps.title: Why the 2.70 gap is no free lunch
steps.why: The gap 34.00 − 31.30 = 2.70 is the reward for bearing the risk that the deal fails (then you lose 6.30 per share). Public news is priced at once.

pitfalls: Computing 31.30 / 34.00 = 92% – that ignores the price after a failed deal.

basis.ref: Do fund managers have skill? · Folien 33–35

prompt: A mutual fund earned 9.4% per year before fees. Its beta is 1.1, the risk-free rate 2% and the market risk premium 6%. The fund charges fees of 1.2% per year. Compute the fund's gross alpha (before fees) and net alpha (after fees). Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Required return = 2% + 1.1 × 6% = 8.6%.
Gross α = 9.4% − 8.6% = 0.80% → the manager has some skill.
Net α = 0.80% − 1.2% = -0.40% → investors only earn the net alpha and lose compared with an index fund. This matches the evidence: positive gross, slightly negative net alpha on average.

steps.title: Gross alpha (before fees)
steps.result: Gross alpha = +0.80% → the manager has some skill

steps.title: Net alpha (after fees)
steps.why: Investors only receive the return after fees.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: The skill is fully eaten by the fees: investors would do better in an index fund. This matches the evidence on mutual funds – slightly positive gross, slightly negative net alpha on average.

pitfalls: Subtracting the fee from the required return instead of from the fund return.

basis.ref: If beta is not enough: more factors · Folie 41

prompt: A stock has the following factor betas: market 1.1, size (small minus big) 0.4, value (high minus low) 0.3, momentum (winners minus losers) −0.1. The factor premiums are 5%, 2.5%, 3% and 6%; the risk-free rate is 3%. Compute the required return with the four-factor model and with the CAPM (market beta only). Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Four factors: 3% + 1.1 × 5% + 0.4 × 2.5% + 0.3 × 3% − 0.1 × 6% = 3% + 5.5% + 1% + 0.9% − 0.6% = 9.80%.
CAPM: 3% + 1.1 × 5% = 8.50%.
The extra factors capture the size, value and momentum patterns the CAPM misses.

steps.title: Four-factor model
steps.why: Required return = rf + sum of (factor beta × factor premium). A negative beta (momentum) lowers the required return.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: The difference (1.3 percentage points) comes from the size, value and momentum exposures that the CAPM ignores.

pitfalls: Adding the momentum term with a plus sign.

basis.ref: Every buyer needs a seller (Jérôme) · Folien 19–21

prompt: Explain why the average investor earns an alpha of zero, and how an uninformed investor can guarantee herself a non-negative alpha.
modelAnswer: All investors together hold the market portfolio, so the value-weighted average of their returns is the market return: the average alpha is zero. Every buyer needs a seller – one investor's positive alpha is another investor's negative alpha. An uninformed investor simply holds the market portfolio (index fund/ETF): she earns the market return, an alpha of zero, whatever the others know or do, at low fees. She only loses if she moves away from the market (e.g. trades on mistakes or pays high fees).
keyPoints: All investors together hold the market → average alpha = 0
Every buyer needs a seller: +α for one is −α for another
Hold the market portfolio / index fund → α = 0
Losses only from deviating from the market or fees

prompt: Define the disposition effect and explain under which condition behavioral biases of individual investors move market prices.
modelAnswer: Disposition effect: investors sell winners too early and hold on to losers too long (they are about twice as likely to sell at a gain; the losers they keep do worse). Individual, random mistakes cancel out across investors and do not move prices. Prices are affected only if many investors make the same mistake (systematic, persistent biases such as the disposition effect, attention/mood effects or herding) and informed investors cannot fully trade against it.
keyPoints: Sell winners too early, hold losers too long
Systematic biases shared by many investors move prices
Only if informed traders cannot fully correct them
